collections.name: The Rise of Greek Civilisation

stops.note: It starts with a rock. Volcanic glass from Melos reaches the mainland by 11,000 BC — which means someone crossed open water to get it, thousands of years before the first city anywhere.
The islands are dry, small and individually poor. That is precisely why their people became the best sailors in the Aegean: everything had to move by sea.
The first distinctive Aegean art. Marble, abstract to our eyes, brightly painted to theirs, and made to lie down in graves.

stops.name: A town before towns
stops.note: On Lemnos, streets, drainage, a public well — and a room with tiered stone benches that may be the oldest council chamber in Europe.
On the mainland, the House of the Tiles: monumental, tiled, full of sealed containers. Then, around 2200 BC, it burns, along with much of Early Bronze Age Greece.
Crete escaped that collapse. Around 1900 BC something new appears there: complexes combining storage, workshops, ritual and — decisively — writing.
The largest of them. Over a thousand rooms, drainage not matched again in Europe until the modern era, and archives in a script we still cannot read.
We can pronounce it and cannot understand it. Around 1,400 short documents survive — far too few to break, without a bilingual text.
Then a town buried alive. Ash preserved Akrotiri to second-storey height, with its wall paintings still on the walls — the closest we can get to standing inside this world.
Europe's first palace civilisation, and the template — architecture, art, administration, religion — that everything after it inherited.

collections.summary: From marble figurines in the Cyclades to the first literate palace states of Europe — how the Aegean became a civilisation.
collections.intro: Nothing about Greek civilisation was inevitable. It begins with islands too poor to be self-sufficient, which forced their inhabitants to become sailors, and ends three thousand years later with a language spoken from Marseille to the Indus. This route follows the first half of that: the emergence of complexity in the Aegean.

collections.name: The Bronze Age and its Collapse

stops.note: Warrior kingdoms on the Greek mainland, with citadels, chariots, and the first written Greek.
Cyclopean walls, the Lion Gate, and shaft graves holding fifteen kilograms of gold. Later Greeks assumed giants had built it.
The paperwork of a state: sheep counts, bronze rations, chariot wheels marked serviceable. All of it survives only because the palaces burned.
The richest archive, in an unfortified palace. Its last tablets record watchers posted along the coast.
Across the sea, the Hittites — who name a place called Wilusa, a king called Alaksandu, and a power called Ahhiyawa.
Nine cities on one mound. Troy VIIa burns around 1180 BC, with arrowheads and unburied bodies in the debris.
Then, within a generation, every Mycenaean palace is destroyed or abandoned. Writing stops. Monumental building stops.
At Ugarit, the last letters were still in the kiln when the city fell. The king writes that his fleet is away and the country is undefended.
Egypt records coalitions attacking by land and sea, travelling with families in ox-carts. Not a raid — a migration.
Drought, earthquake, trade failure, revolt and movement, compounding. Interconnection made these societies rich, and made them fail together.
What follows is three centuries without writing — and the period that quietly invents the alphabet, the polis and Homer.

collections.summary: An interconnected world of palaces, archives and long-distance trade — and the two generations in which all of it failed.
collections.intro: By 1300 BC the eastern Mediterranean was a single system: Mycenaean Greece, Minoan Crete, the Hittites, Egypt, Ugarit and Cyprus, all trading, corresponding and intermarrying. Bronze itself required it — copper from Cyprus, tin from Afghanistan. Within about fifty years almost all of it was gone. This route follows the system, and then its failure.

collections.name: The Trojan War: Myth and Evidence

stops.note: Start with what Greeks believed: a ten-year siege, dated by Eratosthenes to 1194–1184 BC, from which they reckoned their heroic past.
The poem covers fifty days in the tenth year and stops before the city falls. There is no wooden horse in it.
Behind the poem, an oral tradition — formulaic, sung, reshaped over four centuries before anyone wrote it down.
The man who went looking, found something extraordinary, dug straight through the layer he wanted, and embellished the story afterwards.
Nine cities. Troy VI destroyed as if by earthquake; Troy VIIa crammed with storage jars and burned, with arrowheads in the ruins.
Independent evidence: Hittite archives naming Wilusa, king Alaksandu, and repeated friction with Ahhiyawa across the sea.
And the trap. A magnificent gold mask, named for a legend, dating three centuries too early — and the name has never come off.
Whether the commander existed is separable from whether the campaign did. Neither answer follows from the other.
The most famous episode has no early source, no Bronze Age depiction, and enters the visual record in the seventh century BC.

stops.name: Where this leaves us
stops.note: A conflict at Troy involving Mycenaean Greeks is plausible. The Iliad is not a report of it. That is the honest position, and it is more interesting than either alternative.

collections.summary: A case study in how to hold a story and its evidence apart without discarding either.
collections.intro: The Trojan War is the best test of a difficult skill: reading a tradition seriously without believing it. There is real evidence for a real conflict at a real place. There is no evidence for the war of the Iliad. Both statements are true, and the interesting work happens in the gap between them.

collections.name: The World of Homer

stops.note: No writing, no palaces, no monumental building. And, running underneath, singers transmitting stories about the world that had ended.
Then Lefkandi: a fifty-metre building over a warrior cremated in a bronze urn, a woman in gold, and four sacrificed horses. Around 1000 BC.
Not necessarily a person. Milman Parry showed the formulaic epithets are the working technique of singers composing live — tested against living oral poets.
What survived accurately: the boar's-tusk helmet Homer describes in detail had gone out of use four centuries before he sang.
Then vowels. Greeks take a Phoenician consonantal script and reassign unused signs — creating a script learnable in weeks.
And immediately make a joke with it. A small clay cup on an island off Italy, inscribed in verse, claiming to be Nestor's golden one.
A poem about rage that ends with two enemies weeping together over a body. It has never stopped being read.
And its opposite: domestic, non-linear, admiring of lies, and the first European narrative to start near the end.
Beside them, a Boeotian farmer who names himself, names his village, and complains about his brother — the first personal voice in European literature.

collections.summary: How an oral tradition survived three illiterate centuries, and what it preserved along the way.
collections.intro: The Homeric poems describe a Bronze Age that had been in ruins for four hundred years when they took their present form. Some of what they describe is accurate. Some is the poet's own world. Some is invention. Sorting them is one of the most productive problems in classical scholarship.

collections.name: The Persian Wars

stops.note: First, the other side. Twenty-five million people, satrapies, a standardised gold coinage, and a road system crossing 2,700 km in a week.
Its founder conquered Lydia in 546 BC, which brought Persian rule to the Ionian Greek coast — and made a Greek conflict structural.
Athens sends twenty-five ships. Sardis burns. Herodotus has Darius instruct a servant to say "remember the Athenians" at every dinner.
The first answer: hoplites, at a run, thinned in the centre and enveloping the wings. 192 Athenian dead, and a demonstration that Persia could be beaten.
The second invasion. A pass a few metres wide, three days, a mountain path, and a rearguard that stayed. The archaeology found the arrowheads.
Meanwhile, the man who spent a silver windfall on 200 triremes instead of distributing it, and read "wooden wall" as ships.
In the narrows, Persian numbers become a liability. Aeschylus fought here and staged it eight years later from the Persian court's point of view.
The largest hoplite battle ever fought ends the invasion. The initiative passes to the Greeks.
And immediately becomes something else. An alliance against Persia, a treasury on Delos, and within a generation an Athenian empire.
The book that made all this knowable — and invented the idea of asking, and of saying when you are not sure.

collections.summary: Two invasions, four battles, and the moment a fragmented periphery decided it was one thing.
collections.intro: Two things should be held together here. The Greek victory was genuinely improbable and genuinely consequential. And almost everything we know comes from the winners, in a tradition that had strong reasons to make Persia look both enormous and decadent.

collections.name: Athens and Democracy

stops.note: It starts with a debt crisis. Solon cancels the debts, bans enslavement for them, and replaces birth with property as the qualification for office.
Then fifty years of tyranny that, paradoxically, weakens the regional aristocracies and builds the festivals democracy will inherit.
The decisive move: ten artificial tribes, each drawn from three separate regions, so no tribe has a local patron. Social engineering as constitutional design.
Democracy's rubbish. Eleven thousand potsherd ballots — including 190 naming Themistocles, written in fourteen hands.
Elected general year after year. Pay for jurors, so poor citizens could serve. And Thucydides' verdict: in name a democracy, in fact rule by the first man.
What the empire paid for. Nothing in it is straight — the stylobate curves, the columns lean inward and would meet 2.4 km up.
The city itself: perhaps 40,000 citizens, 40,000 resident foreigners, and 60,000 or more enslaved people.
And what visibility cost. The best-documented non-royal woman in Classical Athens reaches us almost entirely through men attacking her.
A democracy that let its most powerful citizens be ridiculed by name, on stage, at a state religious festival.
And one that voted, by a narrow margin, to execute its most famous questioner. Both are the same system.

collections.summary: The most participatory government of the ancient world, and the unfree majority that made it possible.
collections.intro: Athenian democracy was more directly participatory than any modern state, and it excluded women, foreigners and a very large enslaved population. Neither fact cancels the other. This route follows both.

collections.name: Sparta: The System and the Mirage

stops.note: Begin with the founder who probably never existed. Plutarch opens his Life by admitting nothing about him can be stated without contradiction.
Two kings, a council of elders, five annually elected ephors who could prosecute even kings — and no city walls.
The system's most famous product, and its most famous defeat: three days in a pass, then a mountain path, then a stand.
Where the archaeology confirms the story — Persian arrowheads, concentrated on the hillock where Herodotus says the last men died.
Twenty-seven years, and victory purchased with Persian gold — which meant handing the Ionian Greek cities back to Persia.
The admiral who caught the Athenian fleet beached and empty, and installed narrow oligarchies across the former empire.
Then the reckoning. A massed left wing fifty ranks deep, and 400 of 700 Spartiates dead in an afternoon.
And the move that finished them: liberating Messenia, whose enslaved population had farmed the land that fed the whole system.

stops.name: The mirage
stops.note: Spartiate numbers fell from perhaps 8,000 to a few hundred over two centuries. A society that made military excellence its only value could not reproduce itself.

collections.summary: A society organised entirely around war, sustained by mass enslavement — and mythologised almost beyond recovery.
collections.intro: Sparta is the most misunderstood society in the ancient world, partly because it wanted to be. It admitted no visitors, wrote almost nothing, and left its reputation to be composed by foreign admirers writing after its decline. The archaeology and the demography tell a harder story.

collections.name: Alexander's Campaign

stops.note: None of it happens without the father. A broken kingdom in 359 BC, and twenty-three years later, the army that will take Persia.
The instrument: a six-metre pike wielded two-handed, which makes a man nearly defenceless alone and nearly unassailable in formation.
Where it is proved. Philip withdraws in good order to open a gap; the eighteen-year-old Alexander charges into it.
Then Asia. A river crossing under fire, an axe through his helmet, and Cleitus saving his life — the man he would later kill.
Darius manoeuvres brilliantly onto ground too narrow to use his numbers. Alexander charges straight at him; Darius runs.
Seven months building a causeway to an island city. Tyre is still a peninsula because of it.
A limestone ridge between sea and lake, with a natural double harbour. It is still one of the great cities of the Mediterranean.
Open ground, levelled for chariots, every advantage to Persia. A wedge into a gap, and the empire ends. Dated to the day by a Babylonian eclipse record.
Vengeance, or a drunken party with a torch. The excavation confirms an intense fire and cannot say why.
Then the other pattern. Philotas tortured and executed; riders sent ahead to kill his father before word could reach him. No evidence against either.
Monsoon rain, two hundred elephants, and his hardest battle. Bucephalus dies. At the next river his army refuses to go further.
Babylon, June 323 BC. Eleven days of fever, no viable heir, and — within hours — his generals at each other's throats.

collections.summary: Eleven years from the Hellespont to the Indus, and the thirty-two-year-old who never lost a battle and left no heir.
collections.intro: Alexander is easy to narrate and hard to assess. The campaign is genuinely without parallel. So is the body count, and so is the pattern of killing his own generals. Follow the route, and keep both in view.

collections.name: The Hellenistic World

stops.note: Forty years of war among Alexander's generals, ending with three kingdoms and the elimination of his entire family.
Egypt, ruled by Greeks who presented as pharaohs to Egyptians and as Hellenistic kings to Greeks.
The first state-funded research institute: salaried scholars, free meals, and a book-acquisition policy that amounted to confiscation.
Thirteen books from five postulates. Still in schools two thousand years later, and the model of what proof means.
A stick, a well and a measured road. Error under two percent, from a man who never left Egypt.
And the heliocentric proposal that was rejected for a good reason: no observable stellar parallax. It was not measured until 1838.
Hydrostatics, the lever, π bounded to three decimal places — and, in a palimpsest read in 1906, indivisibles that come very close to calculus.
Thirty bronze gears, a Saros eclipse dial, and a pin-and-slot mechanism modelling the Moon's variable speed. Nothing comparable survives for 1,400 years.
Meanwhile, on the Oxus in Afghanistan: a theatre for 6,000, a gymnasium, and the maxims of Delphi carved 5,000 km from Delphi.
One language from Marseille to Kandahar — where a Buddhist emperor addressed his subjects in it.
And an art that abandons restraint entirely: gods and giants breaking out of the frame onto the steps you are standing on.
It ends in Alexandria in 30 BC, with the last ruler of the last kingdom founded by Alexander's generals.

collections.summary: Three kingdoms, one language, and the most scientifically productive period of antiquity.
collections.intro: The Hellenistic age is routinely treated as a decline from Classical Greece. On the evidence it is the opposite: this is when Greek civilisation becomes international, professionalises science, and produces its most technically astonishing objects.

collections.name: Evidence and Doubt

stops.note: Start with survival bias. Every Mycenaean archive we have exists because a palace burned. Records meant to be recycled were accidentally fired.
And with the counter-example: a decipherment achieved from internal patterns alone, then confirmed by a prediction on a tablet dug up afterwards.
Then the limit. We can pronounce Linear A and cannot read it, because 1,400 short texts is not enough and there is no bilingual.
Reconstruction as interpretation: painted concrete, frescoes rebuilt from a few fragments, and a civilisation named after a myth.
Whose head was missing. The crown and the cat came from elsewhere, and the type became so saleable that convincing forgeries entered museums.
A genuinely unlooted royal tomb, and two skeletal studies nine years apart reaching opposite conclusions about who is in it.
An eyewitness clinical description written explicitly so the disease could be recognised again — and we still cannot identify it.
A masterpiece with a fabricated provenance, repatriated in 2008, which changed what museums are allowed to buy.
And a case where the sceptics were wrong: the vapours excavators dismissed turned out to sit above two intersecting faults.
Finish with the man who started it — reporting what he was told, naming his doubts, and being vindicated far more often than his critics expected.

collections.summary: How we actually know things about antiquity — and the celebrated cases where we do not.
collections.intro: This collection is about method rather than period. Every stop is a case where the evidence is unusually revealing about how ancient history is done: what survives, what that survival distorts, and how confident anyone is entitled to be.

quizzes.name: The Bronze Age Aegean

questions.q: Which script was used to write the earliest known form of Greek?
questions.explain: Linear B was adapted from Minoan Linear A to write Greek. Michael Ventris deciphered it in 1952, pushing attested Greek back roughly five centuries before Homer.

questions.q: What is the strongest evidence that Mycenaean Greeks controlled Knossos after c. 1450 BC?
options: The palace was rebuilt in mainland style
The Knossos archives switch to Linear B, which records Greek
Homer says so in the Iliad
questions.explain: Material culture can travel through trade. Administration cannot: if the palace records are kept in Greek, Greek-speakers were running the palace.

questions.q: Why do Linear B tablets survive at all?
options: They were fired deliberately for permanent storage
Destruction fires baked the unfired clay
They were sealed in dry tombs
questions.explain: The tablets were temporary records meant to be recycled annually. Every archive we have exists because a palace burned down — a striking case of survival bias.

questions.q: The Mask of Agamemnon dates to approximately:
questions.explain: Roughly three centuries before any traditional date for the Trojan War. Schliemann's name for it was wishful, and it has proved impossible to dislodge.

questions.q: Which is NOT supported by current evidence about the Theran eruption?
options: It buried the town of Akrotiri
It generated tsunamis that struck Crete
It directly caused the destruction of the Cretan palaces in 1450 BC
Its ash has been identified across the eastern Mediterranean
questions.explain: On the high chronology the eruption is c. 1620–1600 BC — more than a century before the 1450 BC destructions. The two events cannot be directly linked.

questions.q: What do the late Mycenaean water systems at Mycenae, Tiryns and Athens suggest?
options: A prolonged drought was already underway
questions.explain: Three separate citadels independently cut concealed passages to springs outside their walls, late in the period. That is siege preparation.

quizzes.summary: Minoans, Mycenaeans, and the collapse that ended both.

quizzes.name: Evidence and Confidence

questions.q: A claim resting on an inscription carved in stone is classified as:
questions.explain: Epigraphic evidence is text inscribed on durable material. It is often contemporary with the events, which makes it unusually valuable.

questions.q: Coin hoards are especially useful to historians because they:
options: Always name the ruler who issued them
Provide precise dating and show trade circulation
questions.explain: Numismatic evidence dates deposits tightly and maps economic reach. Athenian owls turning up in Egypt tells you about trade no text records.

questions.q: Which confidence level fits "Agamemnon ruled Mycenae"?
questions.explain: The claim comes solely from poetic tradition with no supporting contemporary evidence. Legendary is not a synonym for false — it marks the kind of claim it is.

questions.q: Which confidence level fits "The Parthenon was built between 447 and 432 BC"?
questions.explain: Inscribed building accounts survive recording expenditure year by year. This is about as securely dated as anything in Greek history.

questions.q: Why is "the Library of Alexandria burned down in one catastrophe" classified as debated?
options: No ancient source mentions the Library
Evidence points to gradual decline through several causes
The Library has never been located
The claim originates in the 19th century
questions.explain: Caesar's harbour fire, lost patronage and the expulsion of scholars all contributed over centuries. The single-catastrophe story is tidier than the evidence.

questions.q: A Minoan fresco reconstructed from a few original fragments should be treated as:
options: Direct archaeological evidence for what Minoans depicted
Partly archaeological evidence, partly modern interpretation
questions.explain: The surviving fragments are evidence. The connecting passages are a modern painter's hypothesis, and the two need to be visually distinguishable.

quizzes.summary: How historians classify what they know — and how sure they are entitled to be.

quizzes.name: Classical Greece

questions.q: Cleisthenes' ten tribes were each composed of trittyes drawn from three different regions in order to:
options: Break the link between aristocratic families and local power bases
questions.explain: A tribe with members from city, coast and inland had no single local patron. It is social engineering as constitutional design.

questions.q: What did Themistocles persuade Athens to do with the silver strike at Laurion in 483 BC?
questions.explain: Three years later that fleet fought at Salamis. It also made the poorest citizens, who rowed the ships, politically indispensable.

questions.q: At Salamis the Greeks fought in narrow straits because:
options: It negated the Persian numerical advantage
The Greek ships were faster in open water
questions.explain: In the narrows a larger fleet cannot deploy and ships foul each other. Themistocles reportedly leaked false intelligence to force the engagement there.

questions.q: Moving the Delian League treasury to Athens in 454 BC mattered because:
options: It marked the conversion of an alliance into an empire
Athens needed the silver for coinage
The temple on Delos had burned
questions.explain: Allied tribute then funded the Acropolis building programme. Members who tried to leave were besieged and forced back.

questions.q: Epaminondas defeated Sparta at Leuctra by:
options: Using cavalry to outflank the phalanx
Massing his left wing fifty ranks deep against the Spartan right
questions.explain: It inverted the convention that the best troops go on the right. Around 400 of 700 Spartiates died — a loss Sparta's demography could not absorb.

questions.q: Which best describes the political context of Socrates' trial?
options: Athens was at the height of its imperial power
Athens had recently lost the war and endured the Thirty Tyrants
Macedon had just taken control of Athens
A plague was ravaging the city
questions.explain: Several of his associates had been prominent in the oligarchy. An amnesty barred prosecuting them for it — but not this.

quizzes.summary: Persian Wars, Athenian democracy, and the war that ended it.

quizzes.name: Myth and History

questions.q: Which of these is NOT narrated in the Iliad?
options: The quarrel between Achilles and Agamemnon
The wooden horse and the fall of Troy
questions.explain: The Iliad covers about fifty days in the tenth year and ends with Hector's funeral. The horse comes from the lost Iliupersis and, in full, from Virgil.

questions.q: What has never been found in Minoan art?
questions.explain: The Minotaur is a Greek story about Crete, not a Minoan one. Bulls are everywhere in Minoan art; the hybrid monster is not.

questions.q: Hittite archives support a historical Troy connection by naming:
options: Wilusa, a king Alaksandu, and a power called Ahhiyawa
A ten-year siege of a coastal city
questions.explain: Independent, contemporary, non-Greek documents naming a place and a power. That is evidence for a context, not for the Iliad's war.

questions.q: Poseidon's importance in the Linear B tablets from Pylos is notable because:
options: He receives more offerings than any other deity, including Zeus
He is not mentioned at all
He appears only as a place name
questions.explain: The Bronze Age pantheon was not the Homeric one. Poseidon was pre-eminent at Pylos and was later demoted as the palace states disappeared.

questions.q: Helen received cult worship at Sparta, which suggests:
options: She was certainly a historical queen
She may have originated as a goddess later demoted to a heroine
The cult was invented in the Hellenistic period
questions.explain: Cult worship is a different kind of evidence from epic narrative, and it points the opposite way from the usual assumption that heroes get promoted.

quizzes.summary: Distinguishing what the stories say from what the evidence shows.

quizzes.name: Alexander and After

questions.q: Philip II's key military innovation was:
options: The sarissa phalanx paired with Companion cavalry
questions.explain: The pike phalanx pins the enemy line while heavy cavalry breaks it at an angle — the hammer-and-anvil system Alexander inherited intact.

questions.q: How is the date of Gaugamela known so precisely?
options: A Babylonian astronomical diary records a lunar eclipse eleven days earlier
Coins struck to commemorate the battle
questions.explain: Astronomical records convert to modern dates exactly. It is one of the most securely dated events in ancient history: 1 October 331 BC.

questions.q: Why did Alexander besiege Tyre for seven months rather than bypass it?
options: He could not leave a Persian naval base behind him
It was the birthplace of Darius III
The oracle at Siwa instructed him to
questions.explain: Strategy, not spite. He built a causeway out to the island, which silted up and permanently joined Tyre to the mainland.

questions.q: What did Seleucus obtain from Chandragupta Maurya, and what did it decide?
options: 500 war elephants; the battle of Ipsus
Iron for weapons; the battle of Gaza
A marriage alliance; the siege of Rhodes
Grain shipments; the battle of Pydna
questions.explain: He traded the easternmost provinces for elephants. At Ipsus they screened Demetrius' cavalry out of the battle, and Antigonus was killed unsupported.

questions.q: The Antikythera mechanism is remarkable chiefly because:
options: It bears an inscription naming Archimedes
It uses bronze gearing to model astronomical cycles, unmatched for over a millennium
questions.explain: At least thirty gears, an eclipse dial, and a pin-and-slot device reproducing the Moon's variable speed. Nothing comparable survives for about 1,400 years.

questions.q: Why did the Roman legion defeat the Macedonian phalanx?
options: Tactical flexibility on broken ground where the phalanx line fragmented
questions.explain: Polybius set out the analysis: the phalanx is unbeatable frontally on level ground, and helpless once gaps open. Maniples were trained to exploit exactly that.
